conqueror_tradition: Other: Mongol traditional religion (Tengrism), with Buddhist leanings
source1: Reuven Amitai, 'Hulagu Khan', Encyclopaedia Iranica XII/5, 2004 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hulagu
notes: Hulegu not Muslim: Mongol custom, Buddhist interest, Nestorian wife. Ghazan converted June 1295; Islam proclaimed official religion Oct 1295 and spread among the Mongol elite (Hambly, EBSCO). Tegüder Ahmad briefly Muslim 1282-84. Persian divan used.

source1: Carol Bakhos, 'The Roman Conquest of Judea', Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization - https://www.posenlibrary.com/node/11568
notes: Pompey besieged Jerusalem 63 BCE, made Hyrcanus II high priest and ethnarch under Roman oversight. The Roman ruling elite kept Roman state religion; no adoption of Judaism (Christianity, a third tradition, came centuries later).

source1: Ulrich Braukämper, A History of the Hadiyya in Southern Ethiopia, Harrassowitz 2012 (publisher description) - https://www.harrassowitz-verlag.de/A_History_of_the_Hadiyya_in_Southern_Ethiopia/title_4271.ahtml
source2: Yasin Mohammed, 'Introduction, Expansion, and Practice of Islam among the Muslim Communities of Illubabor', EJOSSAH 21(1), 2025 - https://ejol.aau.edu.et/index.php/EJOSSAH/article/download/13405/9291/26998
notes: Hadiyya a Muslim state fragmented by Oromo expansion from 16th c. Arsi Oromo (who absorbed Hadiya) held Waaqeffanna; Islamization dated to 19th c. (citing Braukämper), beyond 100 years. No centralized court (gadaa); oral culture. Thin evidence.

conquered_tradition: Other: Syro-Hellenistic polytheism (Greek and Aramaean/Syrian cults)
source1: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Dept. of Ancient Near Eastern Art, 'The Seleucid Empire (323-64 B.C.)', Heilbrunn Timeline - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/sleu/hd_sleu.htm
notes: Database value Mesopotamian corrected: Mesopotamia lost to Parthians by 141 BCE; the rump kingdom Pompey annexed in 64 BCE was Syria (Greek cities, Aramaean cults). Romans kept Roman state cult; Syrian cults reached the court only later (218 CE). Tradition correction is inference.

source1: Shainool Jiwa (trans.), The Founder of Cairo: The Fatimid Imam-Caliph al-Mu'izz and his Era, Institute of Ismaili Studies/I.B. Tauris (reading guide) - https://iis.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/the_founder_of_cairo.pdf
notes: Fatimids (Ismaili Shia) conquered Egypt 969 under Jawhar; ruled 'in an overwhelmingly dominant Sunni culture'; few Egyptians became Ismaili. Sunni vs Ismaili counts as same tradition. Large Coptic Christian population persisted.

Pulakeshin I took Vatapi and the Kadamba lands c. 540s; Badami has 6th-7th c. Brahmanical (and Jain) cave temples. Kadambas were a Brahmin-founded Brahmanical dynasty with Jain patronage; Jainism also popular among subjects.

Parantaka I, 'destroyer of Madurai', united Chola and Pandya lands. Pandyas had turned from Jainism to Shaivism; Cholas were Shaiva temple builders (UNESCO, Great Living Chola Temples, https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/250). Both Hindu.

conqueror_tradition: Other: Manchu shamanism (with Tibetan Buddhist patronage)
source1: Tatiana Pang, 'Controversy for State Ideology: Buddhism and Confucianism during the First Manchu Emperor', PIAC 55th meeting, 2012 - https://www.altaist.org/?p=3382
source2: Ronald Gray, 'Promulgation of the Sacred Edict', EBSCO Research Starters, 2022 - https://ebsco.com/research-starters/politics-and-government/promulgation-sacred-edict
notes: After 1644 the Confucian element became predominant in Qing state ideology; Confucian Six Maxims 1652; Song Learning official orthodoxy under Kangxi. Shamanic court rites and Tibetan Buddhism retained (National Palace Museum). Pre-1644 Confucian institutions partly adopted already.
